prompt.context: Your client is in the mining industry. They have just purchased a mountain that has high concentrations of a valuable metal ore. Unfortunately, the mountain is made up of an unusually hard type of rock and none of the commercially available drills are able to penetrate the mountain's surface. Your client's engineers have built a prototype of a drill that could be used to extract the metal from the mountain.
prompt.question: The client is not sure about whether to manufacture the drill and has doubts regarding profitably mining at the mountain. Help the client think through the issue.

clarifying_info.q: Is there any way to mine without having to manufacture the drill?
Is it possible to manufacture the drill that the client has prototyped?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the client can manufacture the drill in-house.

clarifying_info.q: Is it possible to outsource the production of the drill to one of our suppliers or other manufacturers?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, there is a supplier who is capable and willing to manufacture the drill.

framework: Identify the two core issues: (1) which drill option is more cost-effective — manufacture in-house vs. outsource; (2) is mining at the mountain profitable overall
Phase I — Understand the mine plan: useful life, extraction schedule, and production caps
Phase II — Cost analysis for each drill option: fixed setup costs + variable cost per drill x number of drills needed
Phase III — Profitability analysis: total revenue minus total operating costs minus total drill costs for each option
Recommendation: select the lower-cost drill option and confirm overall profitability

questions.prompt: What is the total ore that can be extracted over the life of the mine?
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply the percentage-of-US-production cap to each 5-year period and note the logistical cap of 12,000 tons per year where the percentage-based limit exceeds it.

math.setup: Annual US production = 64,000 tons. Apply caps per period; logistical cap = 12,000 tons/year.
steps: Years 1-5: 10% x 64,000 = 6,400 tons/year x 5 years = 32,000 tons
Years 6-10: 15% x 64,000 = 9,600 tons/year x 5 years = 48,000 tons
Years 11-15: 20% x 64,000 = 12,800 tons/year, but capped at 12,000 tons/year x 5 years = 60,000 tons
Years 16-20: 25% x 64,000 = 16,000 tons/year, but capped at 12,000 tons/year x 5 years = 60,000 tons

questions.prompt: How many drills are needed under each option and what is the total drill cost for each?
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate drills needed from total ore, drill throughput, and drill lifespan. Then apply fixed + variable costs for in-house and variable-only cost for outsourced.

math.setup: In-house: 500 tons/drill/year, 4-year lifespan. Outsourced: 400 tons/drill/year, 2.5-year lifespan.
math.answer: In-house: 100 drills, $40MM total. Outsourced: 200 drills, $50MM total.

questions.prompt: Is the mining operation profitable under each drill option?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total revenue, subtract 20 years of operating costs and drill costs for each option.

math.answer: In-house manufacturing yields $5MM profit; outsourcing yields -$5MM (a loss).

brainstorming.prompt: What risks or additional considerations should the client be aware of?

categories.name: In-house manufacturing risks
ideas: Cost overrun risk on the $30MM facility setup — important to fix construction costs with contractors
Operational complexity of running a drill manufacturing operation alongside mining

categories.name: Supplier relationship
ideas: Proceeding with in-house manufacturing may strain relations with the drill supplier
Client could mitigate by communicating transparently or offering the supplier other business

categories.name: Upside opportunities
ideas: Client could sell its proprietary drill design to other mining companies that operate in similarly hard geological conditions
Licensing or selling drills could generate an additional revenue stream

categories.name: Sensitivity / what would flip the decision
ideas: Higher outsourced drill durability or lower per-drill price could make outsourcing competitive
If in-house setup costs rise above $40MM the economics reverse
Changes in ore price ($325/ton) affect profitability under both options equally

recommendation: The client should manufacture its own drills. In-house manufacturing produces a $5MM profit over the life of the project, whereas outsourcing results in a $5MM loss — a $10MM difference driven by lower total drill cost ($40MM vs. $50MM).
If the client proceeds, it is critical to lock in the $30MM construction cost with contractors to prevent cost overruns that would erode the profit margin.
risks: Cost overrun risk on the $30MM in-house manufacturing setup
Potential deterioration of relationship with the drill supplier
next_steps: Secure fixed-price contracts with construction contractors for the manufacturing facility
Evaluate opportunity to commercialise the proprietary drill design by selling or licensing it to other mining companies
Monitor ore market pricing and extraction rates to ensure the project remains within profitability bounds
